prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Stretch’d and still lies the midnight, Two great hulls motionless on the breast of the darkness, Our vessel riddled and slowly sinking, preparations to pass to the one we have conquer’d, The captain on the quarter-deck coldly giving his orders through a countenance white as a sheet, Near by the corpse of the child that serv’d in the cabin, The dead face of an old salt with long white hair and carefully curl’d whiskers, The flames spite of all that can be done flickering aloft and below, The husky voices of the two or three officers yet fit for duty, Formless stacks of bodies and bodies by themselves, dabs of flesh upon the masts and spars, Cut of cordage, dangle of rigging, slight shock of the soothe of waves, Black and impassive guns, litter of powder-parcels, strong scent, A few large stars overhead, silent and mournful shining, Delicate sniffs of sea-breeze, smells of sedgy grass and fields by the shore, death-messages given in charge to survivors, The hiss of the surgeon’s knife, the gnawing teeth of his saw, Wheeze, cluck, swash of falling blood, short wild scream, and long, dull, tapering groan, These so, these irretrievable.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Stretch, Two, Our

outputs.L1:
Midnight lies stretched and still. Two great hulls rest motionless upon the breast of darkness. Our vessel, riddled and slowly sinking, is being prepared for passage to the ship we have conquered. The captain stands on the quarter-deck, coldly issuing orders through a countenance as white as a sheet. Nearby lies the corpse of the child who served in the cabin; beside it, the dead face of an old salt with long white hair and carefully curled whiskers. Despite every effort, flames flicker above and below. The husky voices of the two or three officers still fit for duty rise amid formless heaps of bodies and solitary corpses, dabs of flesh upon the masts and spars, severed cordage, dangling rigging, and the slight, soothing shock of the waves.

Black, impassive guns stand amid a litter of powder-parcels and a strong, lingering scent. A few large stars shine overhead, silent and mournful. Delicate breaths of sea-breeze carry the smells of sedgy grass and fields from the shore. Death-messages are entrusted to survivors. The surgeon’s knife hisses; the teeth of his saw gnaw. There is the wheeze, the cluck, the swash of falling blood, the short wild scream, and the long, dull, tapering groan.

These remain so—these irretrievable.
outputs.L2:
Midnight lies drawn out and unmoving.  
Two massive ships rest without motion on the dark water.  
Our own vessel is torn through and going down by degrees, while men make ready to transfer to the ship we have captured.  
On the quarter-deck, the captain issues commands with icy composure, his face as pale as linen.  
Close at hand lies the body of the cabin boy.  
There is also the dead face of an old sailor, his long white hair and neatly curled whiskers still visible.  
Flames, despite every effort to stop them, waver both above and below.  
The few officers still able to serve speak in rough, hoarse voices.  
Bodies lie in shapeless heaps, and others lie apart; bits of flesh cling to masts and spars.  
Ropes are severed, rigging hangs loose, and the waves give the ship faint, soothing jolts.  
The guns sit black and unfeeling amid scattered powder packets and a heavy odor.  
Overhead, a handful of large stars shine in silence, sorrowful and still.  
Light breaths of sea air carry the smell of marsh grass and fields from the nearby shore.  
Last messages from the dying are entrusted to those who remain alive.  
The surgeon’s knife hisses; his saw bites and rasps.  
There are wheezes, clucking sounds, the splash of falling blood, a brief frantic cry, and then a long, low groan that fades away.  
All of this is so—fixed, final, beyond recall.
outputs.L3:
The scene presents the grim aftermath of a fierce naval battle fought at midnight. Two ships lie motionless in the darkness, locked together after the violence has ended. The silence that follows the combat feels heavy and unnatural, broken only by the sounds of the wounded, the shifting wreckage, and the sea moving around the damaged vessels. What had been moments earlier a place of noise, fire, and struggle has become a scene of ruin.

The speaker’s own ship has been badly damaged in the fighting and is now sinking. Its structure is shattered, and it can no longer remain afloat. Because of this, the surviving crew must prepare to abandon it and transfer to the enemy ship they have conquered. Victory, however, brings no sense of triumph. The captured vessel becomes not a prize but a desperate refuge, the only means by which the survivors may escape the sea.

All around them are signs of death and injury. Fallen sailors lie across the decks, and the bodies of the dead are scattered among broken weapons, torn rigging, and splintered wood. The horror is made even more painful by the presence of a dead cabin child, a reminder that war destroys the innocent as well as the armed. Gruesome remnants of battle remain everywhere, showing the physical cost of the conflict in shocking detail. The survivors are surrounded by suffering, blood, and wreckage.

Despite exhaustion, shock, and devastation, the captain and the remaining officers continue to give orders. Their duty does not end when the battle stops. They must organize the transfer, care for the wounded where possible, and keep control over the frightened and weakened crew. Their commands create a fragile sense of order amid chaos, even as they themselves are clearly affected by the destruction around them.

The poem emphasizes the irreversible horror of war through vivid sensory details. It does not present battle as glorious or heroic, but as something brutal and permanently damaging. The sounds of pain, the smell of blood and smoke, and the images of mangled bodies and sinking ships all create an atmosphere of deep suffering. By focusing on these details, the poem shows that war leaves behind not honor or celebration, but trauma, loss, and devastation that cannot be undone.
outputs.L4:
The passage presents the aftermath of a naval battle in grim and unforgettable detail. Instead of celebrating victory or emphasizing heroism, it lingers on the destruction left behind: a shattered ship, badly damaged and sinking, surrounded by the signs of violence and ruin. Through vivid sensory imagery, the scene becomes immediate and physical. The reader can imagine the broken timbers, the water pouring in, the smoke, blood, exhaustion, and confusion that follow combat. The ship is no longer a proud instrument of war but a wreck, a place of suffering where survival itself has become uncertain.

The people on board are shown in the same devastated condition as the vessel. The survivors are exhausted, stunned, and weakened by the ordeal, while the dead and wounded lie waiting to be moved to the conquered ship. This detail is especially powerful because it turns attention away from the abstract idea of victory and toward the human beings who have paid for it. The defeated ship may be captured, but what remains is not triumph so much as loss: bodies, pain, fatigue, and the slow, sorrowful work of gathering what is left after the battle.

The passage’s main effect is therefore to strip war of glamour. It does not present combat as noble adventure or glorious conquest. Instead, it reveals war as irretrievable devastation, something that cannot be undone once it has passed through human lives. Even victory appears mournful, because it is surrounded by death and suffering. By focusing on the wounded, the dead, and the sinking ship, the passage makes the cost of battle feel stark and immediate. Its mood is one of grief rather than celebration, showing that the consequences of war remain long after the fighting ends.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a grim naval battle aftermath scene in the style of Walt Whitman, using long free-verse lines and vivid sensory details.
counterfactuals.output:
After the guns have ceased, after the great throats of iron are silent, after the smoke loosens its black hands from the masts and drifts shoreward in rags,

I walk the deck among the splinters and the torn cordage, among the warm pools spreading darkly in the seams, among the boots without owners and the hands still clenched upon nothing,

The sea, that old mother, that vast indifferent nurse, heaves under us green and gray, lifting the wrecks as if they were cradles, lowering them as if they were graves,

And the ship groans, not with battle now but with memory, with the slow complaint of beams split by shot, with the sigh of water entering where no water should be.

O the smell of it!—powder bitter on the tongue, hot metal, salt brine, wet oak, pitch, torn flesh, the sour breath of fear gone stale in the morning air,

O the white gulls circling already, bold and shrill, their wings bright as clean linen over the blackened guns, over the faces turned upward, over the open mouths that answer no roll-call.

Here lies the drummer-boy, his cheek against the deck as if listening for some far parade beneath the planks,

Here the old quartermaster, beard clotted, one eye open to the sky, still stern, still keeping watch where the flag hangs shredded and stubborn,

Here two enemies drift together in the scuppers, their sleeves tangled, their blood mingled in one little river that knows no nation.

The surgeon kneels with red arms, calling softly to those who cannot hear him, cutting, binding, whispering courage as if courage were a blanket to pull over the cold,

And from below comes the knocking of the trapped, faint and terrible, like hearts beating inside the hull, like ghosts asking admission to the day.

The cannon, those terrible preachers, stand dumb in their smoke-stained pulpits, their mouths black, their sermons ended,

The sabres are nicked, the pistols empty, the proud brass dulled with soot, the bright buttons torn away and rolling in bloodied water with chips of bone and glass.

Look there—beyond the rail the enemy ship burns low, a red wound upon the mist, her rigging lit like nerves, her spars falling one by one with a hiss into the sea,

And men swim between us, some crying for rescue, some for mothers, some for God, and some making only the small animal sounds that come when names are lost.

We haul them up by the wrists, by the hair, by whatever part of them remains to be held,

We lay them beside our own, and the deck receives all alike, blue coat and gray coat, foreign tongue and familiar curse, boy’s smooth chin and veteran’s scarred throat.

The sun rises anyway, immense and calm, gilding the smoke, touching the blood until it shines, laying a golden hand upon ruin as if blessing what should not be blessed.

O morning, do you not see? O light, are you blind? You pour yourself over shattered planks and torn banners, over the dead in rows, over the living who envy them for a breath,

Yet still you come, lavish, impartial, filling the broken cups, flashing on the bayonets, making jewels of the salt tears drying on a powder-blackened face.

I hear the sea slap softly at the hull, slap and withdraw, slap and withdraw, washing the names away from the sides of the ships,

I hear the low chant of the wounded, the creak of tackle, the splash of bodies committed to the deep, one after another, each with a weight at the feet and a brief word at the lips,

Down they go, the brave, the foolish, the frightened, the beloved, down through green light and cold silence, past drifting weed and startled fish, to the floor where no trumpet reaches.

And I, standing amid smoke and sunlight, amid victory that tastes of ashes, amid defeat that looks much the same,

I gather them all in my seeing—the captain with his torn sleeve, the cabin-boy with the broken fiddle, the nameless sailor whose blood runs into the sea and becomes part of the tide,

I do not ask who fired first, who struck true, who claimed the waters, who will write the dispatches in a clean hand far from this reeking deck,

I ask only who will remember the weight of them, the warmth leaving the fingers, the last breath mingling with fog, the terrible quiet after the roar.

For the ocean keeps no monuments but motion,

The wave rises, the wave falls, the foam blooms white and vanishes,

And under the keel, under the drifting wreckage, under the gulls and the pale indifferent dawn,

The dead sail on together, without flag, without rank, without hatred, rocked in the dark arms of the sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Whitmanesque poem describing two warships at midnight after a brutal sea battle, with the defeated ship sinking and survivors preparing to transfer vessels.
counterfactuals.output:
At midnight, under the moon’s cold, unpitying lantern, the two ships lay near—  
Not as rivals now, not as thunderers, not as iron-throated beasts of the nation,  
But as vast wounded creatures breathing smoke upon the black sea.

One, the victor, stood scarred and solemn, her sides torn, her rigging loosened,  
Her deck dark with labor, with blood, with the print of hurried feet,  
Her guns still warm, mute now, their mouths dumb after the long bellowing.

The other—O the other!—  
She settled by the bow, slowly, with a grand and terrible patience,  
Her broken masts leaning like trees after lightning,  
Her shattered planks drinking the deep,  
Her flag half-lost in the vapor and spray,  
Yet clinging, clinging, as if cloth too could remember honor.

Around them the ocean rolled on—  
The same ocean that before dusk had flashed with fire,  
That had taken the iron hail and the splintered beams,  
That had received the cries of men without answering,  
Now heaving quietly, immense, indifferent, star-strewn.

Lanterns moved along the decks—small wandering stars in human hands.  
Voices called through the dark, hoarse, practical, alive:  
“Lower away!”  
“Stand by the lines!”  
“Bring the wounded first!”  
And from the sinking ship came the survivors,  
Pale faces lifted from smoke,  
Hands burned, sleeves torn, lips salt-white,  
Men who had cursed the enemy at sunset  
Now reaching toward him at midnight.

I saw them gathered by the rail, waiting their turn,  
The boy with a bandaged brow holding another’s coat,  
The gunner silent, staring back at the place where his comrades lay,  
The officer with his sword gone, his pride not gone,  
The seaman laughing once—only once—at nothing, from sheer wonder of being alive.

Between the ships the boats rose and fell,  
Cradles upon a grave,  
Bearing the bruised, the stunned, the defeated,  
Bearing also something no cannon had mastered—  
The stubborn ember of man within man.

O midnight after battle!  
O strange truce written not by kings but by exhaustion,  
By pity, by the nearness of death,  
By the sight of another’s face under blood and soot!

The victor received them—not with cheers,  
But with blankets, water, hands extended,  
With room made among the wounded of her own.  
For what is victory, after the guns cease?  
What is defeat, when the sea rises for all alike?

Lower she sank—the ruined ship—  
Her ports awash, her great heart flooded,  
Her timbers groaning farewell to the air,  
And the men who had served her watched from another deck  
As one watches a house burn,  
As one watches a mother lowered into earth,  
As one watches a name pass into silence.

Then, with a sigh vast enough for the dead,  
She turned, yielded, vanished—  
The black water closing over beam and banner,  
The bubbles rising briefly like prayers,  
Then nothing but the moon-path broken and restored.

And still the boats moved.  
And still the lanterns glowed.  
And still the living crossed from loss to life,  
From one warship to another beneath the patient stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a 19th-century free verse passage about the aftermath of a naval engagement, including wounded sailors, dead officers, fire, blood, and mournful stars overhead.
counterfactuals.output:
After the thunder of guns had rolled away,  
the sea lay heaving, black and red, beneath the wreckage;  
splintered spars drifted like broken lances,  
and torn canvas hung from the masts  
as if the very winds had been wounded.

Upon the deck the sailors lay,  
some groaning with their hands pressed hard to crimson cloth,  
some staring upward with salt on their lips,  
calling faintly for mothers, for wives, for the green hills of home.  
The ship’s surgeon moved among them with a lantern,  
his sleeves dark to the elbow,  
his face as pale as the moon behind the smoke.

Near the shattered quarterdeck the officers were still;  
their swords were beside them, their bright buttons dulled,  
their commands spent forever in the roar of battle.  
No trumpet called them now,  
no answering cheer rose from the wounded ranks—  
only the crackle of fire  
creeping along the beams like a living thing,  
and the low wash of blood mingling with seawater.

Flames climbed the rigging in red blossoms,  
licking the night, devouring rope and sail;  
the guns, hot and silent, glowed like beasts at rest.  
Overhead, beyond the drifting smoke,  
the stars looked down mournfully—  
cold witnesses, numberless and remote—  
upon the ruin of men,  
upon the torn flag,  
upon the ocean receiving the dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate Walt Whitman’s “The Wound-Dresser” style, but set the poem aboard a damaged ship just after combat, focusing on death, surgery, and the sea at night.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Night-Ship Dresser**

Bearing the lantern low through the reeking passage,  
Through smoke that clung in folds to the beams, through splinters and torn rope,  
I went where the wounded lay after the battle,  
Where the ship, great mother, groan’d in the dark sea-swell,  
Her sides pierced, her masts black against the stars,  
Her deck wet—ah, not with the brine only.

I am old now, I tell you what I saw,  
I tell you not of flags flying nor guns leaping,  
Not of the shout, the trumpet, the fierce onset,  
But of the stillness afterward, the low cries, the surgeon’s knife,  
The faces upturn’d to me in the lantern-light,  
The lips that whisper’d water, mother, home.

The sea was black around us,  
Black and breathing, lifting the broken hull, letting her fall,  
And the moon, half hid in vapors, look’d down coldly,  
While from below came the thick smell of blood, tar, powder,  
And men laid close together as sheaves after harvest.

One I remember, a boy with yellow hair clotted dark,  
His hand yet gripping a piece of shattered rail;  
I loosen’d the fingers gently, one by one,  
I wash’d the wound in his side, I press’d the lint there,  
He smiled as if to ask pardon for dying,  
And died before the bandage was tied.

Another, broad-breasted, bearded, silent,  
Had lost an arm at the shoulder;  
The surgeon bent over him, swift, stern, merciful,  
The saw and the basin were beside him,  
The lamp swung to and fro with the ship’s roll,  
And every shadow seem’d a wave passing over his face.

O hands of mine, how many did ye touch that night?  
How many brows did ye smooth, how many mouths did ye moisten?  
I remember the heat of them, the trembling, the clutching,  
I remember the blood running warm through my fingers,  
And outside, forever outside, the sea washing, washing.

Do not ask me of victory.  
Ask me of the man who call’d for his child in a whisper,  
Ask me of the one who pray’d without words, moving only his eyes,  
Ask me of the dead laid under canvas near the shattered gun,  
Their feet together, their faces pale as foam in starlight.

All night the surgeons labor’d,  
Coats off, sleeves roll’d, faces gray with powder and weariness;  
The knives shone briefly, then were darken’d,  
The needles pass’d through torn flesh, the bandages redden’d,  
The groans rose and sank with the water’s heave.

And I, with my lantern and basin,  
Moved among them as one moves among sleepers,  
Calling each by some tender name though I knew not his name,  
Comrade, brother, brave lad, hold fast—  
Yet some could not hold,  
Some slipped like spent waves from the shore.

Near dawn the wind freshen’d;  
Through a rent in the hull’s side I saw the stars paling,  
And the sea, immense, indifferent, beautiful,  
Taking into itself our smoke, our cries, our dead.  
Then we lifted the bodies, one by one,  
Sew’d in their hammocks, weighted, silent,  
And gave them to the deep.

O night sea, receive them gently!  
O vast dark cradle, rock them tenderly!  
They were young, they were strong, they were afraid, they were faithful;  
They had mothers, lovers, fields, streets, songs,  
And now no wound pains them, no cannon wakes them,  
They descend where no bugle sounds.

Years pass, yet still I am there,  
Still I hear the timbers creak and the wounded murmur,  
Still the lantern swings before me,  
Still the surgeon bends, the blood flows, the sea breathes,  
And I, old wound-dresser of the night-ship,  
Go among them, kneel beside them,  
Bind up the living, close the eyes of the dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, catalog-style poem about a conquered vessel, a calm captain, corpses on deck, severed rigging, and the sounds and smells of a battlefield at sea.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Boarding**

The vessel taken, black flag low,  
her name scraped raw by shot and smoke;  
the captain stands where lanterns swing,  
calm as a bell that will not ring.

Around him: boots in bloodwash,  
splintered oars, a shattered glass,  
charts unrolled beneath the dead,  
a compass pointing anywhere.

Corpses on the deck like cargo—  
blue lips, open hands, cut braid,  
powder burns and torn red sashes,  
faces salted pale as clay.

The rigging hangs in severed loops,  
ropes like snakes with broken spines;  
sails in ribbons slap the mast,  
white flags dirtied into gray.

Listen: gulls disputing ruin,  
water knocking at the hull,  
a wounded man beneath the guns,  
the creak of blocks, the drip, the drip.

Listen: cannon cooling into silence,  
iron ticking in its bed;  
far off, thunder—or more ships firing;  
nearby, flies begin their hymn.

Smell the pitch, the bilge, the brimstone,  
rum spilled sweet through char and salt;  
blood made warm by noonlight,  
tar and sweat and opened wood.

The sea itself stays level,  
green-black, polished, almost kind;  
it gathers splinters, caps, and teeth  
and asks no victor’s name.

Only the captain, still as judgment,  
wipes one hand and lifts his eyes.  
Behind him, conquest counts its prizes:  
mast, men, metal, silence, flies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
